verdict.reasoning: Patient says, “been having some problems with my hearing. I can't really hear very well, and notice that my face has been feeling a bit numb recently,” confirming decreased hearing and facial numbness.
Duration: Patient states, “It's been a few weeks now. About three weeks or something,” matching an approximately 3‑week history.
Laterality of hearing loss: “Just one side. Just on my left side. I've noticed that the hearing's kind of gone down a bit.”
Location of numbness: “it's the left side. It's kind of like around my left ear… feeling a bit numb around here,” supporting left facial numbness around the ear.
Jawline involvement: same description continues, “around my left ear and kind of along here. So like my jawline sort of feeling a bit numb,” confirming numbness along the jawline.

Tinnitus: Patient mentions “Occasionally notice—” and clinician completes “Some ringing in your ear,” then patient later reiterates “like the ringing occasionally,” consistent with intermittent tinnitus.
Dizziness: Patient says, “especially sometimes when I get a ringing, I feel a bit dizzy,” indicating occasional dizziness associated with tinnitus.

Anxiety: Patient says, “because I can panic and you can look online, get a bit frantic… is there something particularly serious… Hopefully nothing so serious I would die from it,” showing clear anxiety about severity.
Weakness: In response to “any weakness or numbness down in the rest of the body at all?” patient replies, “No, no, no, no, nothing like that,” denying weakness elsewhere.
Swallowing: To “Have you had any difficulty swallowing?” patient answers, “No,” denying dysphagia.
Speech: To “have you had any difficulty speaking?” patient says, “No,” denying speech difficulties.
Vision: To “Have you noticed any problems with your vision at all?” patient states, “No, that's all good,” denying visual changes.
Ear pain: To “Any pain in the ear or from the ear?” patient answers, “No,” denying ear pain.
Ear discharge: To “Do you have any discharge coming from that ear at all?” patient says, “No, nothing coming out,” denying ear discharge.
Fever: To “have you had any fever at all?” patient responds, “Nothing like that,” denying fever.
Nasal polyps: Patient says, “I've got kind of been told I had polyps in my nose in the past,” confirming a history of nasal polyps.

Labyrinthitis: Patient recalls, “I think they said ages ago I had something called can't quite remember, but labyrinthitis, something like that,” consistent with a remote history of presumed labyrinthitis.

Transcript notes a nasal spray but not that it is a steroid: “if my polyps are playing up, I've got a spray… they gave me prescription ages ago… Unfortunately, I don't [remember the name].” Calling it an “intranasal steroid spray” adds a drug class not stated.
Rennie use: Patient says, “occasionally get some kind of hearty feeling… I take a Rennie's if I need to,” and later, “sometimes take over like Rennie,” confirming as‑needed use.
Allergy: To “Do you have any allergies to any medication?” patient replies, “No, just latex,” confirming latex allergy.
Family history: “My brother had neurofibromatosis. I think it is,” confirming a brother with neurofibromatosis.
Occupation: Patient states, “Yeah, so I'm a jockey,” and clarifies “like with horses,” confirming employment as a jockey.
Living situation: To “do you live alone?” patient answers, “I live with my partner,” confirming she lives with her partner.
Impact on training: “because of all the kind of symptoms… I've just had to do far less training,” confirming reduced training due to symptoms.
Pets: To “Do you have any pets at all at home?” patient replies, “No pets,” confirming no pets.

Mode of consultation and no exam: Clinician says, “Obviously we're limited in terms of assessment via video portal,” and arranges in‑person exam, indicating this was video only with no physical exam performed.

Symptoms and assessment: Left facial sensory disturbance and hearing reduction, tinnitus, and dizziness are described (“left side… feeling a bit numb,” “hearing's kind of gone down,” “ringing… I feel a bit dizzy”) over ~3 weeks, and clinician notes, “What you're describing might be something called Bell's palsy… in order to… confirm that that might be the diagnosis… neurological examination… make sure there's nothing else going on,” matching this assessment including absence of reported focal motor deficits.

Otologic differential: Clinician plans to “have a look inside the ear, see if there's anything to see within the ear,” in the context of left hearing loss, indicating an otologic differential to be assessed.

Anxiety: Patient’s concern about dying (“Hopefully nothing so serious I would die from it… I can panic… get a bit frantic”) is acknowledged, so including anxiety in assessment is consistent with the transcript.

Same‑day face‑to‑face: Clinician says, “I would like you to be assessed in a clinic today… I'll ask them to book you in for a face to face appointment in one of our clinics within central London,” confirming same‑day GP assessment.

Planned exams and purpose: “we can do what we call a neurological examination… confirm that that might be the diagnosis… have a look inside the ear, see if there's anything to see within the ear,” specifically to confirm or exclude Bell’s palsy and other causes.

Admin and calling support: “I'm going to send a message to our admin team. I'll ask them to book you in… And then you can ring the support team number. I'll leave that number in your notes. You can ring them after five minutes and then they'll slot you into a place that's convenient for you,” matching the described plan.
Further reassurance: Clinician says, “someone will see you and hopefully we'll be able to reassure you further,” indicating intent to provide further reassurance following in‑person assessment.
